newsitem.title: JAPAN: Trade surplus slip to help Japan PM please Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Trade surplus slip to help Japan PM please Clinton.

text.p: Japan's vast trade surplus posted a steep decline for the 21st month in row in August, giving Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto some good news to take to his summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton next week.

Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus, often the source of bitter rows with the United States, fell 31 percent in August from a year earlier to 369.5 billion yen ($3.35 billion), the Finance Ministry said on Wednesday.
The surplus with the United States fell 17 percent to 222.3 billion yen ($2.02 billion).

"The trade surplus is moving in a direction desirable for both Japan and the United States," said Kanami Noda, an economist at Wako Research Institute of Economics. "The two nations still have problems concerning several trade items, but have nothing to worry about on the macro-economic front."
Noda said the declining surplus could give Hashimoto some psychological support ahead of Tuesday's summit in New York.
The trade figures make it more likely that the meeting will focus on the issue of U.S. military bases on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa rather than trade.
The August figure was above the top end of the range of analysts' forecasts of between 160 billion yen ($1.45 billion) and 314 billion yen ($2.85 billion).
"The surplus is still on a declining trend as growth in imports continued to exceed that of exports," a Finance Ministry official told reporters soon after the announcement.
Imports in August grew 16.6 percent from a year earlier, drawing strength from a 53.8 percent jump in oil imports on higher global oil prices. Exports, meanwhile, grew 8.7 percent.

The official said the ministry is closely watching oil imports. "Crude oil made up 8.9 percent of overall imports last year. It is a big chunk and we are keeping a very careful watch over the global crude oil trade and price movements," he said.

The value of imports has been rising rapidly for over two years, helped by structural shifts under which manufacturers in search of lower costs have moved factories abroad and companies have become more dependent on foreign suppliers, analysts said.
But import growth is seen slowing, with the volume of imports in August falling for the first time in two months.

Nobuyuki Saji, a senior economist at Nikko Research Center, said the yen's decline has begun to restrict the pace of the increase in import volume. A weaker yen normally makes imported goods less attractive to price-sensitive customers.
The yen's sharp retreat to 110 yen to the dollar from its record high of 79.75 yen in April 1995 should boost exports by making them more competitive abroad, analysts said.

"You've seen some recovery in export volume due to the depreciation of the yen, which made Japanese exporters recover competitiveness, such as in autos and shipbuilding... I think there is a recovery in export activity in Japan," said Susumu Kato, chief economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Tokyo.

Andrew Shipley, an economist at Schroders Japan, said the slowdown in imports was the main reason the surplus was not smaller, but added that import demand should rise again once industrial output picks up in the fourth quarter of 1996.
The trade data is given only in yen terms. Conversions are at the current dollar/yen rate of 110 yen.
